title: Closing the Loop: An Instructor-in-the-Loop AI Assistance System for Supporting Student Help-Seeking in Programming Education
venue: Proceedings of the 57th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education (SIGCSE TS 2026)
extended_summary:
This paper examines how to provide timely, high-quality help to students in programming courses when AI feedback is scalable but sometimes inaccurate, and human instructors are more expert but time-constrained. The authors ask how often students rely on AI versus escalating to instructors, how long instructor responses take and what students do while waiting, and why students escalate when AI help is insufficient.

The intervention is a hybrid instructor-in-the-loop help system embedded in JupyterLab. Students can request GPT-4o-generated planning, debugging, or optimization hints while working on programming assignments. After receiving a hint, they rate it as helpful or unhelpful; if unhelpful, they can escalate the case to a human instructor, adding notes about what remains confusing. Instructors receive the student notebook, comments, the AI hint, and the escalation notes through a web-based interface and provide follow-up feedback.

The system was deployed in a four-week online introductory Python programming for data science course in a University of Michigan master’s program, with 82 students enrolled. The course contained weekly Jupyter notebook assignments, and one instructor on a three-person instructional team handled escalation requests. The study used system interaction logs, assignment-related behavior data, qualitative coding of bug types and feedback quality, and a small end-of-course survey.

The authors conclude that the hybrid model is feasible and that students used AI heavily: 71 students requested 673 AI hints, while only 16 unhelpful cases were escalated by nine students. Students generally stayed engaged while waiting for instructor feedback, continuing to code and review materials rather than becoming passive. However, the study also found that instructor feedback was not always high quality in difficult cases, especially when the original AI hint was incorrect, suggesting that adding humans to the loop improves coverage but does not automatically guarantee quality. Overall, the paper argues that hybrid AI-plus-instructor support is a practical way to scale help in programming education, while highlighting the need for careful attention to feedback quality and workflow design.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used here as the backend for generating programming hints.
identified_tools.use_case: Used within a hybrid instructor-in-the-loop help system embedded in JupyterLab to generate planning, debugging, and optimization hints for students in a Python data science course; students could rate hints and escalate unhelpful ones to human instructors.

findings.finding_summary: In a classroom deployment with 82 students, 71 students (87%) requested AI hints, generating 673 total hints. Of these, 146 hints (22%) were rated unhelpful, and only 16 of those unhelpful cases (11%) were escalated to instructors, suggesting the AI handled most support requests but still failed in a notable minority of cases.
findings.measure: Help-system usage: number of hint requests, unhelpful ratings, and escalations

findings.finding_summary: AI-generated hints were delivered in approximately 20 seconds, compared with an average wait of 13.5 hours for instructor feedback and 17.8 minutes after the instructor viewed a request. This indicates substantially faster support delivery from the AI component than from human escalation.
findings.measure: Response time for AI hints versus instructor feedback

findings.finding_summary: Debugging hints had the highest rate of being rated unhelpful, with 26% marked unhelpful, and debugging was the only hint type that led to instructor escalation. The paper further reports that escalation due to incorrect AI hints was common: among seven escalations following incorrect AI hints, six (86%) received low-quality instructor feedback, highlighting that incorrect AI outputs clustered in difficult cases.
findings.measure: Perceived usefulness and correctness of AI-generated hint types in programming support

findings.finding_summary: While awaiting instructor responses on 16 escalated cases, students remained engaged: students always continued coding, 87.5% continued coding within the first hour after escalation, 75% watched lecture videos, and roughly half requested additional AI hints. However, only 25% solved the question before receiving instructor feedback, indicating the AI-supported workflow did not appear to induce over-reliance but was insufficient alone for many difficult cases.
findings.measure: Student learning behaviors during wait time after escalation

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical classroom deployment with descriptive and qualitative analyses, but it is not an RCT or quasi-experimental design and does not estimate causal effects on learning outcomes. Findings are primarily usage, timing, and quality observations from one course context.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear operational benefits in speed and adoption, but impact on student learning outcomes is not directly measured and effect sizes are not reported. Reported results are therefore promising but ultimately unclear in educational impact.
